I don't see this law as "the government making laws to regulate a company". I see it as the government doing one of the three things it's actually supposed to do: namely, protecting my property rights.

If I buy a machine from Company X, the machine now belongs to me. I can do whatever I want with it (provided, of course, I don't use it to hurt anyone else, but that's a topic for another day), because I own it. Company X has relinquished its property right in the machine in exchange for fair and valuable consideration (i.e., money).

The way I see it, companies shouldn't be allowed to dictate what their customers can and cannot do with machines or other items that they buy. Either I own the item or I don't, simple as that.

Of course Company X shouldn't have to repair the machine for free, in perpetuity; but that's not what the proposed law mandates. Companies can still offer warranties on their products, and they can also refuse to honor their end of the deal if I don't honor mine, but that's not the same thing as physically preventing me from modifying the machine at all. Warranties are a special sort of contract, which is distinct from the property right in the item itself.

The same argument applies to "rooting" mobile phones. If I own the device, then I can do whatever I want with it. I have the right to execute any piece of computer code--any particular string of 0s and 1s--which the device is physically capable of executing. The phone company doesn't have to let me access their network with an unauthorized device--because, again, that is a contract, distinct from the item itself--but if I do not have root access to the device, I do not own it.

At the very least, the fact that I may not be buying the actual device needs to be made clear up front, before money is exchanged or contracts are signed; because I wouldn't agree to that deal. It could be argued that I didn't agree to that deal.

The government is mandating here that repairability be prioritized over everything else: which might not be the right tradeoff in many cases.

There are times when innovative companies make design decisions that a lot of people of initially dislike because it visibly reduces one of these factors, but greatly enhances other factors. I hate to focus on Apple so much, but their fairly recent decision to remove the headphone jack in favor of the lightning connector was fairly controversial, but allowed them to remove the power amplifier and digital audio converter and saved some of the precious limited space for new components. Not having an extra opening in the case also goes a long way to improve the waterproofing of a device.

Now, on the surface, it sounds good to dictate that batteries must be easily replaceable.
